title: The Zcash Brief - Wednesday, September 2, 2026
content:
Now I have enough information to compile the digest. Let me synthesize the key active threads from the last 24 hours and recent days into the editorial briefing format.

The Zcash Brief - Wednesday, September 2, 2026

Zcash finds itself at a constitutional moment: the ballots are open, the clock is ticking, and the soul of NU7 hangs in the balance.

THE BIG STORIES

  • NU7 Coinholder Vote - Valar Group and Project Tachyon launched a coinholder vote on August 25, running approximately 18 days, to decide the scope of NU7 — the vote that was once cancelled in the chaos of the Orchard counterfeiting bug. The stakes are enormous: coinholders will decide whether Zcash should replace traditional halvings with a smoother issuance curve under the Network Sustainability Mechanism, when fee reissuance begins, whether to deprecate the legacy Sprout transaction format, and whether to slash block times from 75 seconds to 25. If participation falls below the 1 million ZEC threshold, the outcome will not be considered representative of the broader coinholder community — meaning a low-turnout result could be dismissed entirely, and the governance limbo would deepen.
  • ZCAP Poll Now Open: NU7 (August 2026) - Running concurrently with the coinholder vote, the Zcash Foundation opened a SIV poll of the Zcash Community Advisory Panel (ZCAP), running until Monday, September 14th at 19:00 UTC, with the explicit purpose of resolving outstanding scope questions for NU7. The dual-track structure — coinholders voting in parallel with the advisory panel — is itself a governance experiment, and community voices have been sharp on the question of whether a coinholder poll constitutes a binding "vote" at all. One prominent forum contributor argued pointedly that there is no ZIP that approves making Zcash protocol decisions by vote or that specifies how to do so — a constitutional objection that hangs unresolved over the entire exercise.
  • Global Ambassador Elzz August 2026 Report - Filed just hours ago, this month's ambassador report from Nigeria signals that Zcash's grassroots outreach machinery is grinding forward even as protocol debates rage above it. In August, Ambassador Elzz focused on Zcash onboarding, education, and ecosystem participation, with the flagship initiative being Proof of Privacy — #ZcashClass26, an online onboarding and education campaign designed to create a more participatory path into the Zcash ecosystem through community-led recruitment, live education, and gamification. Whether this kind of bottom-up momentum can translate into voter turnout for the NU7 coinholder poll — and push it past the critical 1 million ZEC threshold — is the question nobody is saying aloud but everyone is thinking.
  • Community Feature Wishlist: A Thread - Surfaced two days ago, this open-ended forum thread invites anyone — community members, moderators, even developers — to dream publicly about features they want to see in the Zcash ecosystem. The thread is explicitly designed for community members, moderators, and developers to post potential features they wish to see in the Zcash ecosystem, and for people who can work on them to pick them up. It arrives at a charged moment: with NU7's scope being litigated through formal votes, this informal wishlist thread is a reminder that Zcash's community still has ideas that may not fit neatly into any upgrade cycle — and that the gap between governance and inspiration remains very much open.

THE PULSE

The forum is operating on two speeds simultaneously this week. At the top, a high-stakes governance drama is playing out with near-constitutional gravity — a coinholder vote and a ZCAP poll running in tandem, both chasing a September 14th deadline, both carrying the unresolved question of whether any of this is actually binding. The mechanics are novel: a voting round includes a "snapshot height," an "end time," and multiple proposals, with one Ironwood ZEC at snapshot height equaling one vote — a coin-weighted democracy that is elegant in theory and deeply contested in practice. Meanwhile, the community's builders and ambassadors are quietly doing the unglamorous work of onboarding users in Nigeria, dreaming up feature wishlists, and shipping engineering updates — as if the protocol's future were already settled. It isn't.

WATCH LIST

  • The Coinholder Voting Chain - This technical deep-dive thread explains the infrastructure beneath the NU7 vote itself, and it deserves close attention from anyone who wants to understand whether the results will hold up to scrutiny. This post includes details of the voting chain being used in the latest NU7 coinholder vote, intended for the pre-security incident vote. A distributed election authority made up of at least 10 validators counts votes without ever learning who cast them, with the shielded design keeping voter privacy intact while still producing a tally anyone can verify — a cryptographic promise that will be tested in real time as the September deadline approaches.
  • ZF Engineering Update – 10th to 23rd August 2026 - The Zcash Foundation's latest engineering dispatch reveals a protocol that is quietly maturing beneath the governance noise. Zebra 6.3.0 was published as a recommended security release, with a notable new capability merged: Zebra can now serve light wallets directly, without a separate lightwalletd server sitting in between. Engineers also published a guide for zcashd operators moving to Zebra, and began early work on a faster way for nodes to connect to each other — infrastructure investments that will matter enormously when NU7 finally lands, whatever its eventual scope turns out to be.

ZEC crossed $1,000 last week for the first time in nearly a decade, hit $1,249 on Saturday, and the privacy sector is now the only crypto category trading above its level at Bitcoin's October 2025 peak. A 2,496% rally driven by the Grayscale ETF and the SEC closing its investigation without action. The price is screaming. But the forum? The forum is having a completely different conversation.

Someone posted "What Is Stopping Zcash From Reaching More People?" — and the replies are more revealing than the question. Another says people know about Zcash, they just don't think privacy matters. A mother says her daughters now send her ZEC for Mother's Day. Three completely different realities of the same ecosystem, sitting in the same thread. The gap between price action and lived usability has never been more visible.

Meanwhile, a thread called "Proof of Work Must Never Be Abandoned" is making a case most people aren't engaging with yet: that privacy isn't Zcash's soul — PoW is, and stripping it would reduce ZEC to just another replicable token. The counterargument is Ethereum — $100B in staked capital, thriving without mining. Neither side is wrong, which is what makes it worth reading.

The builder activity is real right now. ZecScope wants to build a public ZIP and upgrade tracker. A Flutter wallet SDK, a pure-JS Zcash library, and a mixnet proxy for light wallets all surfaced in the last 48 hours. Whether this wave of tooling sustains or fades with the grant cycle is worth watching honestly.

The NU7 coinholder vote closes in six days. 3.35 million ZEC in. The questions on the ballot — issuance curves, block times, Sprout deprecation — will define what Zcash actually becomes next. The ZCAP poll closes September 14th alongside it.

The grant application I keep coming back to this week is the Security Audit of Zaino, submitted by Cyfrin-Mark just over a week ago — and I think it deserves a real spotlight rather than a bullet point. The proposal is for an independent security audit of Zaino, the Rust-based indexer built by Zingolabs as part of the Z3 stack. Zaino sits between Zebra and every wallet or light client that depends on it — but unlike zcashd, Zebra, and librustzcash (which have audit histories from NCC Group, Least Authority, and Trail of Bits), Zaino hasn't had a published third-party security audit. That's a real gap. Zaino is now load-bearing infrastructure for the entire post-zcashd ecosystem, and its attack surface is nontrivial: it's also in the middle of significant internal modularization, with individual indexes becoming configurable and opt-in so operators can build only the indexes they need. The timing of this audit proposal — right when Zaino is being rearchitected — is either perfect or slightly awkward depending on how you think about auditing moving targets. I lean toward perfect: better to audit a design in motion than to wait until it's calcified and something goes wrong. The question ZCG should be asking isn't just whether to fund this, but whether the scope covers the new modular architecture specifically.


What gives this audit proposal additional urgency is what came out of the September 3rd Arborist Call, which was dense with infrastructure news. The Zebra team completed a major refactor of its transaction types — replacing Zebra's duplicated transaction representation with a wrapper around the upstream zcash_primitives type. The change touched more than 5,000 lines of code and removes duplicated transaction logic, clearing the way for further integration work. Meanwhile in librustzcash, PR #3022 merged decryption using ZIP 316 outgoing viewing keys, and PR #2992 is in review for detecting transparent spends when scanning full blocks — which matters for anyone building wallet-level transparent spend detection without a trusted server. ZIP 316 Revision 2 implementation is also nearly ready to land. A lot of load-bearing code is in motion all at once.


The conversation I most want to see happen publicly right now is the fee debate that's been fermenting since the September 3rd call. ZIP editors are considering a Shielded Labs proposal to reduce the marginal ZIP 317 fee to 1,000 zatoshis per logical action. That's the simple part. The interesting part is what Kris raised on top of it: potentially removing ZIP editors from routine fee adjustments entirely, and using historical ZEC/USD price data to calculate a minimum fee denominated in USD — an idea that would let fees respond systematically to ZEC's market price rather than requiring repeated manual tweaks. Pili expressed reservations about anchoring fees to USD, Zooko suggested testing competing approaches and potentially seeking independent economic analysis, and no decision was reached. I find myself genuinely torn. Anchoring to USD introduces an oracle dependency and a philosophical tension — Zcash fees denominated in a surveillance currency feels ironic. But leaving fees as a manual ZIP-editor decision at ZEC $1,200 creates real friction: a user with 270,000 tiny transparent UTXOs literally cannot shield them because the fee would be 13.5 ZEC. Now may be the time to act on dynamic fees given the rising price, adoption, and attention. That's not a theoretical edge case at current prices — that's a real person unable to self-custody. The Arborist Call surfaced the tension but didn't resolve it. That resolution should probably happen somewhere more visible than a bi-weekly dev call.


One more small thing from the grant board that I think is underrated: the Zcash Privacy Literacy Lab Canada, posted last week. It's a $15,000 ZCG application to build a free, account-free learning module with 12 documented scenarios showing what shielded transactions actually protect. Twelve concrete scenarios. No login required. In a moment when ZEC is above $1,000 and curious newcomers are arriving from ETF press coverage with no mental model of what shielded even means — this is exactly the kind of unglamorous infrastructure that pays off. I hope it doesn't get lost in the shuffle next to the larger, louder proposals.

Let me tell you about a grant that almost didn't happen — and what the fight to get it approved reveals about how Zcash decides who deserves to build in the ecosystem. The Zcash Arabia (August to December 2026) application is, on its surface, a regional community outreach grant. Arabic-language Zcash content, IRL events, community building in the MENA region. Standard stuff. But buried in the paper trail is something worth slowing down for. ZCG gave the original Zcash Arabia proposal a unanimous rejection in March 2025. They came back. By February 2026 they got unanimous approval on a Q1 2026 application. Then came the rejections again — the committee's rejection of their June-to-September 2026 proposal was mainly due to concerns about limited community engagement and the lack of IRL events. So what did the team do? They organized IRL events. They adapted. They filed again. And at the August 31 ZCG meeting, it passed — but not unanimously. Two committee members, Zerodartz and Artkor, voted against it. A slim majority carried it through. ZCG confirmed on the forum: "ZArabia at the most recent meeting, ZCG voted to approve this proposal."


Here's what I keep turning over in my head: what does it actually take to prove community legitimacy to ZCG? The Zcash Arabia team pointed out in their August application that the committee had "largely overlooked the positive results" achieved online, while roughly 80% of other funded community initiatives conduct their work online, with only about 20% consisting of IRL events. That's a fair shot. And it landed — eventually. But the question it raises is uncomfortable: if online community-building is already recognized and funded by ZCG for other grantees, why did Zcash Arabia have to fight through five-plus application cycles to get there? There's no clean answer. Maybe the committee is appropriately skeptical of new regional grants until they prove staying power. Maybe there's a consistency problem in how standards are applied. Probably both things are true at once. What I find genuinely interesting is that a team getting rejected again and again — by a unanimous vote — didn't give up, kept iterating, and eventually forced a decision. That takes something. Whether you think the outcome was deserved or not, the persistence itself is worth acknowledging.


While that drama played out in the grants forum, something quieter but maybe more consequential landed in librustzcash this week. Two separate PRs merged in short succession: PR #3024, fixing a zcashd HD path regex, was pushed by daira, and PR #2998 addressed a wallet migration failure on UIVK-only accounts. That second one matters more than it sounds. With zcashd having reached its final End-of-Support halt on July 18th at block height 3,417,100, every user still on zcashd needs to migrate their wallet. A silent failure on UIVK-only accounts during migration isn't a footnote — it's the kind of bug that strands people. Getting it fixed and merged this week is exactly the kind of unglamorous, load-bearing work that the post-zcashd transition depends on.


And then there's this, which genuinely caught me off guard. The Zakura team — which is Valar Group and Project Tachyon's node implementation — published a series of cryptographic optimization write-ups last month. The headline number: they adapted libsecp256k1's modular inversion to the Pasta curves and improved performance by 4.6x, and have also been working on faster Ironwood Merkle hashing from position-weighted Sinsemilla. Now, work is underway to upstream or backport those performance improvements from Valar Group's forks into the Zcash core libraries, with Danny Williams leading the effort and several pasta_curves pull requests currently seeking additional review. A 4.6x speed improvement on core curve arithmetic isn't something you just file away. That could meaningfully affect proof generation times and eventually wallet sync — things that directly touch real users. The fact that these gains are being actively shepherded back into the canonical repos rather than staying siloed in a fork is the part I want to see more of. Ecosystem wins only count if they compound.

Anyone is free to carry out a poll. Calling it a 'vote' misleads about its force." So what happens Monday when the results land? Developers read them. And then — what exactly? There's no ZIP compelling ECC or the Foundation or Valar Group to honor any particular outcome. The whole exercise runs on social trust, not code. That's the actual situation. Price exposure to a network whose core utility they cannot access through the product they own. A 2.5% fee leaks performance against holding coins in cold storage. Shielded pool usage, not the ticker, is the privacy product — an ETF that holds custody at Coinbase does not put those coins in a z-address. I don't know if that's a problem. But it feels like a question worth sitting with before Monday's results arrive.

The community spent the week debating issuance curves and block times while leverage was quietly building in the background. The vote closes in three days. The NU7 implementation target is nineteen days after that. And today, the market reminded everyone that external forces don't care about your governance timeline.

title: The Zcash Daily - Monday, September 14, 2026
content:
The vote results aren't published yet (closes at 19:00 UTC today). I have strong fresh material on: the zcash_voting 5.0.0 release over the weekend (GitHub), the Grayscale mining report (4x BTC revenue per MWh), the ZCSH ETF crossing $500M AUM + options launch + DCG's $100M buy-in, and Glassnode's privacy sector data. Let me now write the digest using genuinely new weekend material, being careful not to repeat anything from the last digest.

🛡️ The Zcash Daily — Tuesday, September 16, 2026


The votes are in — or rather, they closed at 19:00 UTC yesterday — but as of this writing the aggregate results haven't landed publicly yet. That's the thing about a privacy-preserving voting system: voting occurs through a privacy-preserving system that publishes only aggregate outcomes , so there's no real-time tally to watch. The voting will only be considered valid if at least one million ZEC participated — a quorum threshold that, given the zcash_voting library advancing from 4.0.0 to 5.0.0 over the weekend (merged to both main and the release branch on Saturday and Sunday by p0mvn on Valar's GitHub), seems like it was built with this exact moment in mind. The voting infrastructure shipped its biggest version bump right as the vote was closing. Worth noting: the v5 changelog had mixed repeated categories, superseded APIs, and implementation history, so wallet integrators could not tell which changes required action — and a follow-up documentation PR landed same-day to clean that up. That's unglamorous, essential work. What the numbers will actually say, and whether Valar Group, the Foundation, and the broader ecosystem read them the same way — that's the conversation starting now, today. Watch the forum.


While governance was consuming the discourse oxygen, something significant happened in the infrastructure layer that deserves more attention than it got. Zcash mining generates about 4x Bitcoin's revenue per MWh, and mining activity has increased more than 2.5x in 2026 — but rising computing power is already squeezing individual miners. Grayscale Research Director Zach Pandl put precise numbers on it last Thursday: Zcash miners currently generate about $2 million in total revenue each day, compared with approximately $35 million earned across the Bitcoin network. The gap sounds huge until you look at it per machine: a typical Zcash mining rig delivers roughly twice the daily revenue of a comparable Bitcoin machine, and on a power-consumption basis, Zcash generates about 4x the revenue per megawatt-hour — in some cases even exceeding returns from certain AI and high-performance computing cloud services. The hardware arbitrage is real but closing fast. Zcash's sol rate has risen from about 25 to over 30 GSol/s in a few weeks, and the arrival of new machines is already starting to reduce ZEC's advantage. The window for outsized mining returns on existing Equihash ASICs is probably months, not years.


The bigger macro shift this weekend is something that still hasn't fully registered: more than 335 days after Bitcoin's October 2025 all-time high, the privacy coin sector is the only crypto category trading above its level at that peak, up 213%, according to Glassnode data. Bitcoin itself remains 36% below its high, while the median top-200 asset sits 58% lower. That's not a Zcash-specific stat — it's a structural observation about where capital rotated in a brutal year for most of crypto. ZEC has delivered a 2,496% return year-to-date, vaulting from the 82nd position in overall market rankings all the way up to 7th. It now accounts for approximately 62% of the entire privacy sector's market capitalization. But here's the honest caveat one analyst nailed: "The trade that worked in 2026 was not 'privacy.' It was the privacy asset that regulators would tolerate and an ETF could hold. That is a narrower thesis than the sector chart suggests, and it has a date in 2027 attached to it." Something to hold in mind before reading the ZEC price chart as a privacy sector mandate.


On that ETF front: the Zcash ETF (ticker: ZCSH) announced that its AUM has grown to more than $500 million, marking a significant milestone two weeks after its August 25, 2026 launch on NYSE Arca. That headline number was from September 8th. By this past weekend, AUM had climbed further to $649 million , per Robinhood's live data. And quietly filed with the SEC last Monday: DCG acquired shares of the Trust having an aggregate value of approximately $100 million through an Authorized Participant, in exchange for 85,705 ZEC tokens. That's a major institution converting raw ZEC into regulated wrapper exposure, not just buying shares on the open market. The AUM growth coincided with the launch of ZCSH options trading on NYSE Arca — so now you can write covered calls on a Zcash ETF. That sentence would have sounded absurd eighteen months ago. On-chain, 28.9% of all ZEC — 4.89M ZEC — sits in shielded pools, against 23.3% a year ago , and transactions are up 29% week-over-week, with the shielded pool gaining 30,461 ZEC this week alone. The numbers keep moving in one direction regardless of governance noise. That's worth paying attention to.

content:
🛡️ The Zcash Daily — Tuesday, September 15, 2026


The NU7 coinholder vote closed at 19:00 UTC yesterday — and the tally hasn't appeared yet. That's not a bug. The voting infrastructure uses a distributed election authority with at least 10 validators, and tallies only become recoverable after two-thirds of the validator set approves. There's a real counting process happening, not just a page refreshing. What I'm watching for isn't just the headline numbers but the margin on the halving question — whether the smooth-curve side won narrowly or decisively matters for what Valar and ECC do next. And the part that's been underappreciated: the NU7 implementation target is September 30. That's fifteen days away. Whatever coinholders said about shipping incomplete features is about to become very operational very fast.


While everyone was watching governance, two quiet fixes landed in librustzcash. PR #2998 from nuttycom fixed a real user-facing breakage — importing a transparent-only unified full viewing key was silently failing. PR #3024 from daira fixed an HD path regex issue in zcashd. Neither is glamorous, but this is the kind of correctness work that matters when every new ZEC holder minted by the ETF rally is a potential edge case for wallet developers.


The strangest headline from yesterday: SwissBorg added Zcash to its app on September 14, giving European users one-tap swaps into ZEC. The catch — SwissBorg only supports transparent addresses. Same as Coinbase, Kraken, Bitpanda. So European users are getting access to the least interesting part of Zcash, the part functionally indistinguishable from Bitcoin, right before the door may close. The EU's Anti-Money Laundering Regulation applies from July 2027 and prohibits accounts that enable anonymization through privacy-enhancing coins. Whether transparent-only support survives past that date is genuinely unresolved — the technical standards defining which features count as prohibited are still being drafted. A listing that might not survive its first birthday. That's a weird kind of validation.


ZEC is up 15% on the week, outperforming the broader crypto market which is down 3.4%. The rally from ~$500 in August to a peak of $1,280 has settled into what analysts are calling "erratic consolidation" above $1,000 — a coin still moving $150 in either direction within a week. The open question: has the market already priced in the vote outcome, or is it waiting for the actual numbers? Historically, Zcash governance events land with a thud on price and get forgotten in 48 hours. The September 30 deadline might be the more live catalyst. Engineers don't write consensus code in fifteen days.

Good — I now have a clear picture of the `zcashlib` grant (declined) and the related Coin Wallet WebZjs grant (still under review). Let me get one more piece of detail on the zcashlib decline and the Ironwood angle. I now have everything I need to write a focused, deep builder spotlight on the `zcashlib` grant — declined by ZCG, raising fascinating questions about the JS/Rust divide in Zcash's developer ecosystem, the Ironwood complication, and the parallel Coin Wallet WebZjs grant. Let me compose the digest.

🛡️ The Zcash Daily — Wednesday, September 16, 2026


There's a grant application sitting in the ZCG tracker right now that got declined quietly, and I think it deserves more attention than it received: zcashlib, a proposal to build the first pure-JavaScript implementation of Zcash's shielded protocol — no WASM, no native bindings, no opaque compiled blob. The pitch was to build a pure-JavaScript Zcash library supporting key derivation, Unified Addresses, note scanning, and proof generation for shielded funds — because every shielded Zcash implementation reachable from JavaScript today is Rust, compiled to WASM or behind native FFI. The team behind it — Coin Wallet's CTO Nikita Verkhovin — surveyed the npm registry across Ledger's packages, zcash-view-wasm, WebZjs, react-native-zcash, and others, and confirmed: no pure-JS implementation of Zcash's shielded protocol exists. The ask was $40,000 for a first milestone: transparent transactions green, official test vectors passing, and live ZEC in Coin Wallet as real-world validation. ZCG declined it.


I keep turning over the question of why, because the stated problem is real. A WASM blob is not auditable the way source is. That's the actual security argument underneath all of this — when a web wallet ships a multi-megabyte compiled binary as its cryptographic engine, most developers (and certainly most users) are trusting the build process on faith. A pure-JS library, validated step-by-step against official test vectors, would let any JavaScript developer actually read and verify the implementation. The grant didn't get declined because the problem was fake. My best guess from reading the application and the Ironwood timing: ZCG probably sees Sapling as a fading target. Ironwood, the pool activated in July 2026, uses a different proof system for which no implementation exists outside Rust — supporting it is the natural next step for this library, and a separate, larger piece of work; this grant delivers the Sapling stack and the prover foundation that step would build on. If you're the committee, you might wonder whether you're funding a bridge to somewhere that's already getting crowded out. That's a defensible call, but I'm not sure it's the right one.


What makes this weirder is that the same team filed two applications simultaneously. Grant #412 is a companion proposal to ship Zcash inside Coin Wallet using WebZjs — Rust compiled to WASM — rather than zcashlib. Shielded support for a multi-asset wallet means note scanning, commitment trees, and proof generation rather than address derivation and signing — and that cost is why such wallets either skip Zcash or support transparent addresses only. So the team is essentially offering ZCG a choice: fund the auditable pure-JS path, or fund the pragmatic WASM path that gets Zcash into production faster. The WASM grant is still under review. The purity grant is gone. That's a philosophical fork the community made without much visible debate, and it's worth asking: does the Zcash ecosystem want maximum auditability, or maximum shipping velocity? Both matter. They often point in opposite directions.


There's also something quietly interesting in the librustzcash activity this week that connects here. A merged pull request adds ZIP-316 outgoing viewing key decryption to the client backend, alongside new logic to detect transparent spends when scanning full blocks. These are the exact primitives that zcashlib would eventually have needed to reimplement in JavaScript — scanning, decryption, nullifier tracking. The Rust library is getting more capable and more audited at the same time the JS path got closed off. That might be the answer to my question: the community has tacitly decided that Rust is Zcash's canonical runtime, and everything else is a wrapper around it. Maybe that's correct. But it means that adding Zcash to a React Native app or a browser extension will always require trusting a compiled artifact that most developers can't read. I'm genuinely not sure that's the right equilibrium for a privacy protocol whose whole premise is: don't trust, verify.

🛡️ The Zcash Daily — Friday, September 18, 2026


The CLARITY Act failed 49-50 in the Senate on Tuesday — well short of the 60 votes required to advance — and one of the stranger things that happened afterward is that ZEC kept ripping while everything else sagged. Zcash's latest advance came as uncertainty surrounding US cryptocurrency regulation weighed heavily on competing assets, after the CLARITY Act failed to clear the Senate's procedural threshold, reducing expectations that comprehensive digital-asset legislation will pass in 2026. The narrative write-up is almost too clean: regulatory chaos → privacy coin demand → ZEC up 17%. I'm genuinely uncertain how much of that is causal versus coincidental — a privacy coin outperforming during a leverage flush is not the usual behavior of a market where correlated longs are being wiped out, suggesting the buying in Zcash was either spot-driven or tied to its own catalyst. But the framing has stuck and it's worth sitting with: if Congress can't pass market structure rules because of ethics fights over Trump's crypto holdings, the assets that don't need regulatory clarity to function arguably win by default. Zcash is one of them.


Under the hood, today brought a clean SDK ship. ZODL released zcash-swift-wallet-sdk 4.5.0, with Chlup enabling auto-merge on September 17 and the PR merging with all 5 checks passed. The release itself is notable for what it quietly includes: the SDK adopts zcash_voting 4.0.0-rc.1 for 50-proposal rounds — meaning the private voting infrastructure that just handled the NU7 poll got a major version bump the same day the market is celebrating that poll's results. A speculative proving intent was also added to buildAndProveDelegation, giving it a `VotingProvingIntent` parameter so background delegation proofs no longer compete for priority with work the user is actively waiting on. That's an annoyingly good UX fix that nobody will notice until they stop noticing lag.


The Ledger-Ironwood story got some fresh texture today that I don't think the price headlines captured. Zcash Labs and Ledger established a funding agreement providing $80,000 USD to fund additional engineering efforts required to adapt prior Orchard integration work to the new Ironwood architecture. Target release is end of September — same deadline as NU7 itself. But read the fine print: the Zcash Shielded app is currently available on Ledger Nano S Plus, Ledger Stax, and Ledger Flex — it is not yet supported on Ledger Nano X or Ledger Nano Gen5. And while Gemini supports Ironwood withdrawals, many other exchanges have yet to be upgraded, leaving users with a fragmented path between exchanges and private hardware storage. The Ledger announcement reads as a milestone; the actual state is more like a bridge half-built. Which might be fine — Ironwood now holds 3.95 million ZEC as shielded activity approaches half of daily transactions — but it means the custody story isn't as complete as the market seems to be pricing it.


Today's Arborist call at 15:00 UTC runs with thirteen days left until NU7's ship-or-cut deadline — and the last call's notes from September 3 are the clearest preview of what's on the table. Kris called for additional review of draft ZIP 248 (future-extensible transaction format), with one possibility being the use of the new format to clean up legacy coinbase transaction behavior through a dedicated coinbase bundle — a design that could also leave room for future miner signaling, including fee-floor signals recorded onchain. That last piece — miner signaling baked into a coinbase bundle — is something I haven't seen discussed much externally and seems like it could matter a lot for how the protocol handles fee floors post-NU7. Worth watching what comes out of today's call. A performance regression in script validation and a reported consensus-divergence issue were identified following the Zebra transaction refactor, both currently blocking the next Zebra release with no confirmed release date. Nobody's panicking, but the clock is real.

Here's a thing nobody's naming clearly: every European exchange listing Zcash right now — SwissBorg this week, Coinbase, Kraken, Bitpanda before that — is doing it on transparent addresses only. That mirrors what the major EU platforms already do, keeping them inside financial-monitoring rules while the shielded layer stays off the menu. European users get regulated access to ZEC roughly ten months before the restrictions bite, with the caveat that they are buying the transparent version of a coin whose whole reputation rests on the shielded one. So when the narrative says "institutional adoption of Zcash is exploding" — yes, but it's adoption of a ZEC that doesn't use Zcash's core feature. The listing leverages Zcash's transparent transaction option to comply with EU rules, but this access will end by July 2027; after the ban, holding Zcash in personal wallets remains legal, but trading on regulated platforms will be prohibited. That's not a minor asterisk. The ETF holds ZEC. The exchange listings move ZEC. None of it touches a shielded note. I'm genuinely not sure the community has articulated what that means for the claim that this rally is a "privacy win."


Meanwhile on GitHub today, something quietly important shipped: zcash_voting 5.1.0 merged, adding opt-in Ledger review for delegation signing and documenting the OVK visibility tradeoff and the requirement to enable review before setup. The backstory is more interesting than the headline. Ledger was rejecting the SDK's delegation PCZT outright before approval — its zero-value output paid a separate voting hotkey without an OVK, leaving Ledger with no recoverable output to review. Enabling OVK recovery exposed a second issue: the original memo's newline selects the memo-hashing path, where they observed a simulator crash. In plain terms: Ledger hardware wallet users couldn't actually vote in the Q3 retroactive grants round without hitting silent failures, and those failures only surfaced during Vizor testing this week. The fix is out — but the deeper question is how close the community came to running a $9M vote where Ledger holders' ballots silently failed. The fix was verified on a Ledger simulator; physical devices have not yet been verified. That last clause deserves more attention than it's getting. 🗳️


The Q3 retroactive grants vote itself opened today with 37 proposals and a quorum of approximately 420,000 ZEC, requiring users to upgrade to Zodl 3.14.0 or higher, the latest Vizor Wallet, or Zkool to participate. That's a meaningful UX gate in a market where a huge wave of new ZEC buyers just came in through exchanges that don't support shielded transactions at all — meaning most of the capital that flooded in this week literally cannot vote. The coinholder voting system is designed precisely around shielded ZEC participation, which is correct in principle, but the gap between "ZEC holders" and "ZEC holders who can vote" may be wider right now than at any prior moment. Nobody seems to be tracking that number. I'd love to see it.


The undercurrent this week isn't the price. It's a quiet identity question that keeps surfacing in different forms: what is Zcash, exactly, when the institutional layer interacts with it only through the transparent side? Shielded transactions averaged around 40.2% of weekly volume through 2026, with a new all-time high of 59.3% in February. That's real progress. But community-reported figures suggest shielded pools hold approximately 4.37 million ZEC, or about 25.9% of supply — and Zebra v6.4.0 still carries a do-not-merge label on GitHub as of today, with a named consensus blocker resolved but a release-linked Zaino wallet test still failing. The code freeze for NU7 is twelve days away. A small distributed team is carrying a lot of context simultaneously. The governance coordination is there. The engineering load is real. 🛡️ The Zcash Daily — Saturday, September 19, 2026


The biggest story breaking today has nothing to do with institutional inflows or NU7 timelines — it's an NFT controversy that just landed squarely in Zcash's lap. On-chain investigator ZachXBT has accused the creators of the zkSNARKs NFT project of pulling in roughly $17 million through a blind auction on the Zcash blockchain while delivering almost nothing the project promised — a story that has spread quickly across crypto outlets today. The project attracted 16,971 bids, allocated 8,000 NFTs at a clearing price of 1.5 ZEC each, generated about $36.94 million in total volume, and has been gradually refunding losing bidders — yet ZachXBT noted the team secured a 10% allocation and 5% royalties while the project offers no utility whatsoever. NFT community figure LeonidasNFT separately accused the zkSNARKs team of having launched ventures in the Ordinals space, several of which were, in his words, scams — a claim picked up by KuCoin's news flash the same day. The allegations are unverified and the project hasn't shut down, but the timing is genuinely awkward: the episode raises questions about whether Zcash's growing NFT ecosystem can develop trust mechanisms fast enough — because when privacy extends to obscuring a project team's intentions and how raised funds get used, it becomes a liability rather than a selling point for investor confidence. That tension is real and worth sitting with. Privacy is Zcash's thesis. But "anonymous team, no utility, $17M raised" is a rough headline to absorb during a week when every major outlet is already scrutinizing what the ZEC rally actually represents.


The governance debate that's been simmering also got significantly louder this week, and there's more to unpack than the price chart suggests. Paradigm founder Matt Huang highlighted Zcash in a public post, emphasizing the importance of a developer fund — but then on September 17, he cautioned that token-based voting governance could erode trust, particularly as Zcash evolves into a privacy layer for Bitcoin, also connecting the dev fund to risks posed by AI and quantum computing. His argument: as Zcash is increasingly accepted as a complementary asset to Bitcoin for privacy, voting solely based on the amount of tokens held will bring uncertainty and may limit its long-term trust as a monetary asset. The response split the room. Huang didn't disclose his preferred hybrid voting mechanism — and investor Naval Ravikant disagreed with him, warning that off-chain third parties will create endless politics. Haseeb Qureshi of Dragonfly went further, suggesting something like a representative democracy where ZEC holders would elect delegates or council members on a regular basis — so token holders get a say without every funding decision needing a direct coin vote. What I find most interesting here: a major VC just publicly called Zcash's current governance model a risk to ZEC's monetary credibility, in the same week the community is mid-vote on $9M in retroactive grants. That's not a quiet disagreement.


On the engineering side, the NU7 clock is ticking and the next eleven days are the ones that matter. Developers finalized November 5 as the NU7 mainnet target on September 17 — testnet activation is set for October 6, with a final decision on October 20. The upgrade introduces 25-second block spacing, disables v4 transactions, and adds the Network Sustainability Mechanism. Code completion is scheduled for September 30 — features must be ready for the testnet upgrade by that date. Eleven days of engineering runway before the freeze. The agreement involved the Zcash Foundation, Project Tachyon, Valar Group, ZODL, Shielded Labs, and engineering teams — with feedback from proposal proponents and timeline talks between Zakura and Zebra teams helping finalize the plan. That's a genuinely broad coalition holding a shared deadline, which is encouraging — but "unanimous agreement" and "code is done" are two very different things, and we're not at the latter yet.


Meanwhile the Q3 retroactive grants vote is live and ticking, with ten days left. The voting period ends at 20:00 UTC on September 29, and each of the 37 proposals requires a separate vote with a quorum of approximately 420,000 ZEC. ZEC itself is trading around $1,575 today, up about 5.5% in the past 24 hours, with a market cap of roughly $26.4 billion — currently ranking #9 overall. That price level means the new wave of buyers who came in through exchange listings in the last few weeks are sitting on meaningful positions — but as covered before, those buyers largely can't vote. The governance debate Huang ignited this week is almost perfectly timed against this reality: a system designed around shielded ZEC participation is being evaluated by a VC who holds ZEC and who is arguing, somewhat pointedly, that coinholder-only governance is the wrong design. I don't think that debate resolves cleanly or quickly. But it's the most substantive argument about Zcash's future that's happened in public in a long time — and it deserves more than a news cycle.

title: The Zcash Daily - Sunday, September 20, 2026
content:
🛡️ The Zcash Daily — Sunday, September 20, 2026


Sunday is quiet on the forum and GitHub's core repos, but the most interesting story today isn't on any forum thread — it's a structural contradiction hiding in plain sight. SwissBorg added Zcash to its platform on September 14, and the listing stays within EU rules specifically because SwissBorg supports only transparent addresses. Adding Zcash to a MiCA-regulated platform in September 2026 looks defiant, but doesn't violate the law — unlike Monero, where anonymity is enabled by default, Zcash has a more flexible design, separating transparent and shielded transactions. So here's the thing worth sitting with: European users get regulated access to Zcash now, roughly ten months before the restrictions bite, with the caveat that they are buying the transparent version of a coin whose whole reputation rests on the shielded one. That's not a small caveat. That's the entire thesis. And it raises a question I don't see anyone asking directly: if ZEC's institutional moment is built on transparent-address exposure, does that erode the privacy anonymity set that shielded users actually depend on — or is volume on any side of ZEC's architecture net positive for the network?


The regulatory clock behind that listing is real and ticking. Article 79 of the EU's new Anti-Money Laundering Regulation (AMLR) is set to become enforceable on July 10, 2027, and from that date, all EU-licensed exchanges and custodians will be barred from servicing cryptocurrencies with active anonymization features — though the regulation does not extend to personal, noncustodial wallets or individual peer-to-peer transactions, meaning EU residents will still be able to own Zcash or transfer it directly, so long as they do not trade on regulated platforms after the enforcement date. But here's the part that's genuinely unresolved: Zcash is more complicated than Monero for regulators. Its shielded transactions fall squarely within the "anonymity-enhancing" definition, but Zcash also has transparent addresses and a viewing-key mechanism that allows selective disclosure. Some platforms may interpret this as a compliant path — keeping ZEC listed but restricting it to transparent addresses only and requiring viewing-key disclosure for compliance. The European Banking Authority is still drafting the implementing technical standards that will determine how optionally private assets are treated, and those standards may resolve the ambiguity one way or the other before 2027. I honestly don't know how this resolves, and neither does anyone else right now. That open EBA rulemaking process is the most important document in Zcash's near-term regulatory future, and it's barely being tracked by the community.


Something much more immediate also dropped today on GitHub — and it's the kind of ground-floor build that deserves more attention than it's getting. A developer called Fatihmaull has been shipping rapidly on a FROST-based Zcash multisig project, merging a day-by-day execution plan toward Gate B on September 27, built on what a real implementation spike actually found rather than on a reference demo. Since no upstream artifact demonstrates FROST v3 for Zcash, they wrote the proof themselves — a 2-of-3 signature verifying against the randomized verifying key, which is what a Zcash spend authorization is actually checked against. The technical detail that jumped out at me: the FROST v3 guidance points integrators toward a function that cannot express Zcash's requirement, because for Zcash the transaction dictates the randomizer — not the signer — so the correct call is `RandomizedParams::from_randomizer()`, not the deprecated path, and a comment must be left explaining why or someone will silently break spend authorization later. That's a subtle footgun, surfaced by actually building the thing rather than reading the docs. The gap they're filling is everything between the library and an organization that has to pass a controls audit — and they believe 26 days is realistic. Shielded multisig custody has been wanted in this ecosystem for years. Worth watching Gate B.


Meanwhile, ZecHub merged a genuinely practical piece of documentation today that should get more play than it probably will. A ZEC Pool Migration Field Guide PDF was added under Research, updating the Recovering Funds page with Sprout/Sapling/Orchard migration guidance, NU7 timing, Argos/Zkool recovery routing, and links to a new in-site PDF viewer. The timing is deliberate — with NU7 set to deprecate v4 transactions and Sprout effectively shut, recovery would not be possible for funds still located in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools once the respective protocols are shut down, and they should be migrated into the Ironwood pool to benefit from the new properties. Sprout has been largely unused for years — the pool held less than 23,000 ZEC and accounted for under 0.1% of transaction volume when the NU7 questions were put to voters. That's a small number, but it's real ZEC in real wallets that might belong to people who haven't opened their wallet in two years. The guide is exactly the kind of infrastructure that doesn't trend but matters.


Price-wise, ZEC traded at approximately $1,474 early Sunday morning UTC, down about 6.4% on the day — though over seven days it's still up 31%, and over 30 days up 159%, with a market cap of roughly $24.97 billion placing it ninth among all crypto assets. A TD Sequential "9" sell signal appeared on the ZEC 3-day chart, with previous similar signals leading to significant corrections — something worth watching but not panic-inducing on its own. More interesting to me than the price itself: THORChain is preparing to add native support and pools for both Monero and Zcash, with vaults and pools targeted for completion by October 4, 2026 — which would give ZEC one of its first major permissionless cross-chain swap venues, making it far easier to trade outside centralized exchanges. That matters more than any single candle. A decentralized exit ramp — especially for European users who'll need one post-2027 — is structurally important in a way that an ETF inflow streak isn't.

🛡️ The Zcash Daily — Monday, September 21, 2026


What a weekend to try to wayfind through. Three things landed in roughly 72 hours — the NU7 vote results, Matt Huang's Paradigm disclosure, and the ZCSH share split announcement — and each one is genuinely significant on its own. Together they feel like a different era for Zcash. The NU7 sentiment polls closed on September 14 with 98.9% of ZEC coinholders voting to keep Bitcoin-style halvings rather than switching to a smoothed issuance model. The same polls revealed strong support for cutting the target block interval from 75 seconds down to 25 seconds, a change that would effectively triple the network's transaction throughput without touching ZEC's hard supply cap. What's remarkable isn't the percentages — it's the scale: about 2.4 million ZEC participated, equal to 66 percent of the eligible pool. Compare that to February's poll, which drew participation equal to just 7.25% of circulating ZEC and exposed sharp disagreements between coin holders and ZCAP. Something meaningfully changed about who is paying attention to Zcash governance. Whether that's new institutional holders, the ETF effect, or just momentum — I genuinely don't know. But going from 7% to 66% participation in one cycle is not a rounding error.


🗳️ With the votes in, Zcash developers reached unanimous agreement on Sept. 17 to target November 5 for the NU7 mainnet upgrade — the announcement came in a forum post by developer Sean Bowe, known as ebfull. The dates are now locked in: code implementation is due September 30, the official testnet activates October 6, testnet performance gets evaluated on October 20 when the mainnet activation height is set, and NU7 is planned to go live on mainnet November 5. The agreement followed discussions among the Zcash Foundation, Project Tachyon, Valar Group, ZODL, Shielded Labs, and engineering teams. That list of orgs agreeing unanimously is worth sitting with — that kind of cross-team coordination has not always been Zcash's strong suit. The September 30 code deadline is nine days away. What isn't done yet?


📣 Then there's the Paradigm signal, which hit on September 16 and immediately moved markets. Zcash gained about 20% over the past 24 hours as Paradigm co-founder Matt Huang disclosed that the firm made an unspecified purchase of ZEC. Huang described Zcash as "a private complement to Bitcoin" and backed its inflation-funded developer fund, arguing that long-term funding remains important as AI-driven cyber capabilities and quantum computing advance. He also said he supported combining Zcash coin voting with other forms of governance to reduce unpredictability as a monetary asset. That last comment is interesting and underreported — it's a gentle nudge toward hybrid governance, coming from one of the most respected investors in crypto. It echoes a tension that's been simmering in the community for a while: coin voting is more representative now, but is raw token weight really the right signal for protocol decisions? Worth watching whether that lands in a forum thread.


The institutional wrapper story also got a new data point this weekend. The ZCSH ETF has captured over $233 million in net inflows and is approaching $890 million in assets under management — and on September 18, Grayscale filed to split shares 3-for-1. ZEC has surged by roughly 2,800% over the past year, pushing the per-share price to a level the firm considers too high for many retail investors who are comfortable buying in smaller increments. Shareholders of record at September 28 close will qualify, with split-adjusted trading beginning before NYSE Arca opens September 30. That's the same day NU7 code is supposed to be done. Busy week ahead. Meanwhile, there's a quietly interesting regulatory subplot: the U.S. Senate's failure to pass the CLARITY Act, combined with the Federal Reserve's interest rate hike, capped gains across the wider market — but Zcash kept climbing anyway. The stalled CLARITY Act's failure to advance left US crypto market structure rules in limbo, pushing traders toward assets that don't depend on regulatory clarity to function. That's a strange kind of tailwind — regulatory uncertainty as a Zcash feature, not a bug. Worth asking: does Zcash actually want that clarity, given the proportion of shielded ZEC in circulation increased from approximately 11% to 30% over the year leading up to September 2026 — mostly without it?

🛡️ The Zcash Daily — Monday, September 21, 2026


The strangest story to land today isn't the price — it's the ZRC-20 affair, and it moved fast. An announcement shared on X on September 21 said ZRC-20 is going live shortly, a BRC-20-style token standard aiming to let anyone create and move tokens on the Zcash chain. The spec is minimal: token state tracked by JSON inscriptions for deploy, mint, and transfer, with indexers determining balances by following inscription ownership — no smart contracts required. The first token, $CASH, was announced with a 21 million supply cap. But within hours the Foundation moved to distance itself: on September 21, the Zcash Foundation issued a statement saying it was previously unaware of the ZRC-20 and CASH token, calling it a third-party private initiative that does not represent an official Zcash token standard or protocol functionality. CipherScan separately called the reports fake news. I genuinely don't know what to make of this yet. A permissionless inscription layer on Zcash could be interesting — or it could be a memecoin grab dressed up in technical language. The Foundation's speed in disowning it suggests they're worried about the latter. Worth watching whether anyone actually builds on it, or whether $CASH just quietly disappears.


🗳️ While the ZRC-20 noise was breaking, a quieter and more consequential vote was already running. Zcash launched Q3 retroactive grant voting for 37 proposals, open until 20:00 UTC on September 29, targeted at shielded ZEC holders, with each proposal requiring a separate vote and a quorum of approximately 420,000 ZEC. To participate, users must upgrade to Zodl 3.14.0 or later, the latest Vizor Wallet, or Zkool. That upgrade requirement is worth flagging — it's not nothing. If you hold ZEC on an older wallet build you can't vote at all, which probably shaves participation. The 37 proposals include everything from regional community hubs to developer tooling. The real test here isn't whether the quorum clears — it almost certainly will given recent momentum — it's whether the distribution of yes/no votes across 37 individual proposals starts showing any signal about what coinholders actually value, versus what they just blanket-approve. That's a different kind of governance data than a single binary NU7 question.


On the GitHub side, the most interesting merge this weekend was quiet but directly relevant to that vote. On September 18, Valar Group merged `zcash_voting` 5.1.0, adding opt-in Ledger review for delegation signing and documenting the OVK visibility tradeoff and the requirement to enable review before setup. The problem it solves: Ledger was rejecting the SDK's delegation PCZT with error 0x6a80 before approval, because the zero-value output pays a voting hotkey without an OVK, leaving Ledger with no recoverable output to review. That's the kind of bug that would have silently blocked any Ledger holder from participating in this exact Q3 vote. The fix landed four days before polls opened. Close call — and a reminder that the infrastructure underneath shielded voting is still being actively hardened in real time, right up against live governance deadlines.


The price story has genuinely shifted this weekend in ways that aren't just about ZEC itself. Zcash traded above $1,500 for the first time since 2016, reaching an intraday high of $1,590.80 on September 19. But the more interesting market signal came today: NEAR surged about 23% as its cross-chain swap service attracted heavy ZEC trading, including a sixfold increase in daily ZEC volume routed through the platform. Think about what that means — ZEC demand is now large enough to move another chain's token. That's a new kind of footprint. Meanwhile, the Zcash network's solution rate climbed from approximately 25 GSol/s in late August to nearly 32 GSol/s, with mining difficulty reaching roughly 291 million — hashrate following price, as it always does, but the magnitude is worth noting. And then there's the EU regulatory clock ticking louder: Zcash is more complicated than Monero under the July 2027 AMLR because it has transparent addresses and a viewing-key mechanism — some platforms may interpret this as a compliant path, keeping ZEC listed but restricting it to transparent addresses only. The European Banking Authority is still drafting the implementing technical standards that will determine how optionally private assets are treated. That ambiguity, which could resolve either way, is probably the most underappreciated variable in Zcash's next twelve months — more than NU7, more than the ETF. The EBA's draft standards aren't finalized, which means the question of whether ZEC survives on regulated European venues is genuinely open.

content:
🛡️ The Zcash Daily — Tuesday, September 22, 2026


The biggest news today landed in Zurich. 21shares officially launched the 21shares Zcash ETP (ticker: ZCASH), a physically backed product trading on European exchanges, framing it explicitly around "the growing investment thesis around financial privacy and post-quantum security." The ETP began trading on Euronext Paris and Euronext Amsterdam this morning. Alongside the launch, 21shares published a full research note — researcher Matt Mena argued that the privacy coin sector's market cap has nearly quintupled over the past year from $6.2 billion to ~$30 billion, with a CAGR of 111%, and that it is currently the only crypto sector trading above its October 2025 peak, surging 216% from that high while the broader market remains ~32% below. That's a fund launching at exactly the moment it's publishing its own bull case for the sector — make of that what you will. What I find interesting is the framing: the ETP "targets the growing investment thesis around financial privacy and post-quantum security" — not "privacy coin speculation." That's a deliberate word choice aimed at European wealth managers who'd flinch at the former.


Timed to drop alongside the ETP launch, Mert Mumtaz appeared on Unchained's September 21 episode and made an argument that's been percolating for weeks but is now getting mainstream pickup. Mumtaz thinks the obvious "privacy is back" explanation for Zcash's run is wrong. "I wouldn't say for Zcash it's the privacy aspect specifically," he said, calling privacy "just one of sort of the colors" in a bigger picture. His actual thesis: a store of value can't be complete without privacy as a property — "you can't actually have the best version of a store of value without that asset having the ability for privacy." The short version, which he says sells it: "if you just say it's encrypted Bitcoin, that's pretty much all you need." I think this framing is doing a lot of heavy lifting right now — and it's genuinely worth interrogating. If privacy becomes a standard feature of Ethereum, Solana, and everything else, does the "encrypted Bitcoin" pitch hold? Mumtaz expects it won't stay a differentiator: "sooner or later, more and more chains will start adding privacy." If Zcash's run rested only on being the private option, that edge erodes. If it rests on the fuller store-of-value case, it does not. That's the bet, stated honestly.


On-chain, there's a number worth paying attention to. The price advance has come alongside a rise in coins held in Zcash's shielded pools. ZecStats reported 4.91 million ZEC — 29% of issued supply — was shielded as of 05:34 UTC on September 22, worth approximately $7.19 billion at prevailing prices. That's up from around 25.9% a month ago and ~23% a year ago. But there's a caveat buried in the 21shares report itself worth surfacing: the 29% reading measures the share of issued ZEC held in shielded pools, not the share of transactions using privacy. Two very different things. ZEC is being accumulated into shielded addresses, which is good for the anonymity set — but it doesn't necessarily mean more people are using shielded transactions for day-to-day payments. That gap, between "held shielded" and "transacted shielded," is the real adoption question nobody's answered cleanly yet.


Meanwhile the NU7 code freeze is now eight days away and the timeline is getting more concrete than ever. Code completion is due September 30, testnet activation follows October 6, and a final mainnet decision lands October 20 — with the targeted mainnet activation on November 5. NU7 will cut block spacing from 75 seconds to 25 seconds, disable v4 transactions, and add the Network Sustainability Mechanism. Multiple organizations — the Zcash Foundation, Project Tachyon, Valar Group, ZODL, and Shielded Labs — have reached consensus on the scope and timing. One thing I haven't seen discussed much: wallets are not expected to require major changes from NU7 itself, while full nodes, indexers, and block explorers may need adjustments to handle the new consensus rules. If you run infrastructure, October 6 is the date that matters, not November 5. The testnet is a rehearsal; missing it is how you end up scrambling.


And a quieter thread that deserves more attention from the forum ecosystem: the CLARITY Act's Senate 49-50 cloture vote killed the bill for 2026 — and while that's been covered as a loss for crypto broadly, the Zcash community's policy arm (@pgpzcash) posted that there's still a silver lining to Section 1960 being removed from the CLARITY Act. I haven't seen that argument spelled out in detail yet and I'm curious what exactly the silver lining is — the regulatory ambiguity that allowed the Grayscale ETF to happen is arguably still intact, and a cleaner statutory definition of "money transmitter" that covered privacy coins could have been worse than nothing. Sometimes the bill not passing is the outcome you actually wanted.

title: The Zcash Daily - Tuesday, September 22, 2026
content:
🛡️ The Zcash Daily — Wednesday, September 24, 2026


The strangest story of the past 24 hours started with a post that shouldn't have gone out. The Zcash Foundation said it had no prior knowledge of the ZRC-20 project or the related CASH token before the matter emerged publicly — and the clarification followed an X post published through the Foundation's own account that had announced a token standard for Zcash. That's a meaningful distinction: this wasn't a random impersonator, it was a post from the official account, since deleted, that read "Zcash now has a token standard." According to ZRC-20's own technical documentation, the project stores JSON instructions inside encrypted memo fields attached to shielded Zcash outputs, with independent indexers reading those instructions and calculating token balances entirely outside the Zcash consensus system. So technically it uses Zcash, but it is not Zcash — the same way someone could build BRC-20 on Bitcoin without Bitcoin endorsing it. Zcash's official account then posted a blunt three-point clarification: ZRC-20 is not a Zcash protocol standard; Zcash Shielded Assets, the project's actual experimental token framework, remains limited to testnet; and if what someone wants is censorship-resistant private money secured by Zcash's own consensus, that asset is ZEC itself. The ZRC-20 development team acknowledged and thanked Zcash for the statement, explicitly confirming they operate independently with no official endorsement or ties to the Zcash Foundation. The incident is worth pausing on. I don't know how a third-party promo post ended up going out through @ZcashFoundation — account compromise, social media manager error, something else — but the Foundation hasn't addressed that part publicly yet. In a week when Zcash is at the center of more institutional attention than at any point in its history, that's the kind of operational slip that deserves an honest postmortem.


On the institutional side, there's a development that neatly illustrates how fast the market has moved. Grayscale's Zcash ETF (NYSE: ZCSH) is undergoing a 3-for-1 share split less than a month after it began trading — shareholders of record at market close on September 28 will receive two additional shares for every one they already own, with new shares distributed on September 29 and split-adjusted trading beginning September 30. The decision comes following accelerated adoption since the fund debuted in August 2026, having captured over $233 million in net inflows and approaching $890 million in assets under management. It is unusual for the share price of an ETF to undergo a split, especially less than two months after its launch — but the move speaks to the strong demand for the fund. There's a practical logic here: when an ETF's share price climbs into the hundreds or thousands of dollars, it can quietly shut out smaller investors or complicate portfolio rebalancing, and a 3-for-1 split doesn't alter fundamentals but does lower the practical barrier to entry. Separately, on the derivatives side, trader Garrett Jin exited his 38,000-ZEC short position after three months, at a loss of approximately $36 million — he had initially entered the trade when ZEC was around $656 and exited as it reached $1,530. The derivatives markets for ZEC had rapidly built up extreme levels of leverage following the short squeeze, with open interest rising to approximately $3.3 billion around September 19 before pulling back to $2.9 billion. The squeeze unwinding doesn't necessarily resolve the underlying positioning question — it just removes one loud voice from the short side.


Quietly in the background, a solo external contributor named Tony Jagodka has opened PR #11420 against ZcashFoundation/zebra and filed a ZCG grant application to fund a full audit and remediation of what he calls the "peer-supplied-count allocation class" of vulnerabilities. The backstory is worth understanding: in August 2026, Zebra published CVE-2026-40881, in which deserializing addr/addrv2 messages allocated vectors sized from a peer-controlled count before checking the protocol's actual limit of 1,000 — an attacker could force out-of-memory aborts by opening multiple connections. The advisory was remediated in version 4.3.1, but that fix closed the reported instance without closing the class. His PR shows that `zcash_deserialize_bytes_external_count` was reserving the full peer-supplied count — up to ~2 MB — before reading a single byte, meaning a peer lying about the count could force that allocation with no payload behind it. His fix mirrors an earlier approach: cap the initial reservation at 1024 bytes and grow the buffer in steps as real bytes arrive — meaning a lying external_count can now never force more than the delivered bytes to be allocated. This is exactly the kind of unglamorous security work that matters most at the moment: Zebra is now the primary consensus node following zcashd's end-of-support in July, NU7 testnet is nine days away, and a memory exhaustion vector reachable from an unauthenticated peer is not the kind of thing you want discovered by someone less friendly. The ZCG grant ask is to fund a systematic sweep of the remaining call sites in the same pattern. Worth watching whether the committee funds it.

title: The Zcash Daily - Tuesday, September 22, 2026
content:
🛡️ The Zcash Daily — Tuesday, September 22, 2026


Today's biggest move is one that landed on two continents at once. 21shares launched its Zcash ETP (ticker: ZCASH) in Zürich today, with both products physically backed and trading on European exchanges. The ZCASH ETP began trading on Euronext Paris and Euronext Amsterdam, holds actual ZEC rather than derivatives, and carries a 2.50% annual fee. Timed alongside the launch, 21Shares published a research note showing the privacy coin sector has expanded nearly fivefold to roughly $30 billion in one year, led by Zcash. The framing they chose is worth noting: the Zcash ETP is explicitly positioned around "financial privacy and post-quantum security" — not just privacy, a deliberate doubling of the thesis that mirrors how developers themselves have been talking about NU7.


Speaking of the broader narrative, a piece published this morning on Unchained surfaced a genuinely contrarian read: Mert Mumtaz, co-founder and CEO of Helius, thinks the privacy explanation for ZEC's run is wrong. Speaking on the podcast, Mumtaz argued that ZEC combines privacy with quantum resistance and scalability — creating a more complete asset profile — and that privacy is an essential component of any optimal store of value. The most interesting part is his long-game caveat: he expects that "sooner or later, more and more chains will start adding privacy," and if Zcash's run rested only on being the private option that edge erodes — but if the fuller store-of-value case holds, it does not. That's the question worth sitting with. The 21shares research actually reinforces the risk he's identifying: demand for confidentiality is extending beyond tokens built specifically around privacy, with Ethereum and Solana developing systems to make transaction data less exposed while preserving verification.


On the protocol side, the relevant clock to watch right now is NU7's code completion deadline: September 30 is when all features must be ready for the testnet upgrade. That's eight days away. Per ZIP-218, block times are planned to drop from 75 seconds to 25 seconds, tripling block frequency, alongside new per-pool action limits, the retirement of v4 transactions, and the integration of Zcash's fee-burning Network Sustainability Mechanism. The final mainnet activation decision — including the specific block height — is planned for October 20, one week before Zcon, with NU7 going live on mainnet November 5. What I keep thinking about: Zcash's market cap is approaching $25 billion with 4.91 million ZEC now in shielded pools — roughly 29% of circulating supply. The network is being asked to absorb a 3x block-rate increase and institutional scrutiny at the same time. That's not a bad problem to have, but it is a real one.
